lessons.title: Active and passive voice
lessons.description: Recognise active and passive constructions and preserve meaning when changing voice.
lessons.content: In the active voice, the subject performs the action: “The team planted trees.” In the passive voice, the receiver of the action becomes the subject: “Trees were planted by the team.” The passive form uses a suitable form of be with a past participle, such as was planted or are made. Use it when the receiver or result is more important than the doer.
learning_objectives: Identify the doer and receiver of an action in a sentence.
Distinguish active voice from passive voice.
Change a simple active sentence to passive voice while keeping its tense and meaning.
prerequisites: Identify subjects and objects in simple sentences.

explanation_sections.title: How the two voices differ
explanation_sections.body: The active sentence usually follows doer + verb + receiver: “The learners cleaned the room.” In the passive version, the receiver leads: “The room was cleaned by the learners.” The words by the learners may be left out when the doer is unknown or not important.

explanation_sections.title: Keep tense and agreement
explanation_sections.body: When changing voice, keep the original tense. “The class collects bottles” becomes “Bottles are collected by the class”; “The class collected bottles” becomes “Bottles were collected by the class.” The passive verb must agree with its new subject, and the past participle follows the form of be.

explanation_sections.title: Quick recap
explanation_sections.body: In the active voice, the subject does the action; in the passive voice, the subject receives it. When changing voice, keep the tense and make the verb agree with the new subject.

worked_examples.prompt: Change “The caretaker locked the gate” to passive voice.
worked_examples.solution: The gate was locked by the caretaker.
worked_examples.reasoning: The gate receives the action, so it becomes the subject. Locked is the past participle, and was keeps the past tense.

lessons.author: ElimuQuest Curriculum Team

questions.prompt: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
options: The pupils watered the seedlings.
The seedlings were watered by the pupils.
The pupils are watering the seedlings.
The pupils will water the seedlings.
questions.correct_answer: The seedlings were watered by the pupils.
questions.explanation: The receiver, the seedlings, is the subject, followed by were and the past participle watered.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of “The chef prepares the meal.”
options: The meal is prepared by the chef.
The meal was prepare by the chef.
The chef is prepared by the meal.
The meal prepares the chef.
questions.correct_answer: The meal is prepared by the chef.
questions.explanation: The meal receives the action, and the present-tense passive uses is with the past participle prepared.

questions.prompt: Why might a writer use “The broken window was repaired yesterday” instead of naming who repaired it?
options: The person who repaired it may be unknown or unimportant.
Passive sentences never use verbs.
The writer wants to change the past into the future.
A window can perform the action of repairing.
questions.correct_answer: The person who repaired it may be unknown or unimportant.
questions.explanation: The passive voice can focus on the receiver or result when the doer does not need to be identified.

lessons.title: Direct and reported speech
lessons.description: Report what someone said by adjusting pronouns, tense and time expressions where needed.
lessons.content: Direct speech gives a speaker’s exact words in quotation marks: “I am ready,” said Ali. Reported speech tells what the speaker said without quoting the exact words: Ali said that he was ready. When the reporting verb is in the past, pronouns and verb tenses often shift to match the reporting situation.
learning_objectives: Distinguish direct speech from reported speech.
Change pronouns and verb tense appropriately when reporting a statement.
Use reporting verbs and punctuation correctly in simple examples.
prerequisites: Recognise pronouns and present and past verb forms.

explanation_sections.title: Reporting a statement
explanation_sections.body: In direct speech, quotation marks enclose the speaker’s words. In reported speech, quotation marks are not used; a reporting verb such as said or explained introduces the message. If the speaker says “I”, the pronoun may change to he or she according to who spoke.

explanation_sections.title: Adjust tense and time carefully
explanation_sections.body: With a past reporting verb, present simple often changes to past simple: “I need help” becomes She said that she needed help. Present progressive often changes to past progressive. Time words may also change when the reporting happens later: today can become that day. Make these changes only when the reporting context requires them.

explanation_sections.title: Quick recap
explanation_sections.body: Direct speech gives a speaker?s exact words; reported speech conveys the message without quoting it. Adjust pronouns and, where the context requires, tense and time expressions.

worked_examples.prompt: Report the statement: “We are practising for the concert,” the learners said.
worked_examples.solution: The learners said that they were practising for the concert.
worked_examples.reasoning: We changes to they because the learners are being discussed, and are practising shifts to were practising after the past reporting verb said.

lessons.author: ElimuQuest Curriculum Team

questions.prompt: Choose the correct reported form of: “I enjoy reading,” Mary said.
options: Mary said that she enjoyed reading.
Mary said, “she enjoyed reading.”
Mary says that I enjoyed reading.
Mary said that he enjoy reading.
questions.correct_answer: Mary said that she enjoyed reading.
questions.explanation: I changes to she because Mary is being discussed, and enjoy changes to enjoyed after the past reporting verb said.

questions.prompt: Which feature belongs to direct speech?
options: The speaker’s exact words are enclosed in quotation marks.
The speaker’s words are always changed to the past tense.
The sentence must begin with the word that.
The speaker is never identified.
questions.correct_answer: The speaker’s exact words are enclosed in quotation marks.
questions.explanation: Quotation marks show the exact words spoken in direct speech.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct reported form of: “I will visit you tomorrow,” Peter said to Amina.
options: Peter told Amina that he would visit her the next day.
Peter told Amina that I will visit you tomorrow.
Peter told Amina that she would visit him yesterday.
Peter said Amina would visit him the next day.
questions.correct_answer: Peter told Amina that he would visit her the next day.
questions.explanation: I refers to Peter and you refers to Amina; will commonly shifts to would and tomorrow to the next day in this later report.
